title: Freshwater turtle

names.note: Dictionary: 'freshwater turtle'. A general word; the dictionary does not split it by species.

scientificName: Chelidae: Emydura, Myuchelys, Elseya and Chelodina species

identification.basis: The dictionary defines ngujay simply as 'freshwater turtle' and keeps ngawiya for the sea turtle. It is most likely a general word for all the river turtles. On the upper Mitchell those are chiefly the northern yellow-faced turtle (Emydura tanybaraga) and the saw-shelled turtle (Myuchelys latisternum), with snapping turtles (Elseya) and the northern snake-necked turtle (Chelodina rugosa) also recorded. Whether speakers had separate words for these is not recorded.

summary: **[Ngujay](word:ngujay)** is the Kuku Yalanji word for the freshwater turtle [ref:hershberger1982], the river turtle of the creeks and waterholes, as opposed to *[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)*, the [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle). Across North Queensland Roth found river turtles caught by hand or with small [nets](entry:nets); on the Palmer River they were killed by breaking the neck [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives **[ngujay](word:ngujay)** 'freshwater turtle' [ref:hershberger1982]. It is a different animal and a different word from the [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle), **[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)** [ref:hershberger1982]. The shell of a turtle is **[kadan](word:kadan)**. The more general word **[dumbul](word:dumbul)** covers 'any hard covering such as bark of a tree, crust of bread, shell of turtle' [ref:hershberger1982].

Older English writers called river turtles **'tortoises'**, and Roth and Anderson both use that word. When they write 'freshwater tortoise', they mean ngujay [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
Two common river turtles of the north are these; both are recorded on the upper Mitchell [ref:ala].

- **Northern yellow-faced turtle** (*Emydura tanybaraga*). A short-necked turtle with a shell up to about 28.5 cm. A light yellow band runs from the eye back to above the ear, and another from the corner of the mouth along the neck. The shell is light to dark brown with a yellow or white rim, and the belly plate is bone-coloured [ref:wp-emydura].
- **Saw-shelled turtle** (*Myuchelys latisternum*). The back edge of the shell stays **saw-toothed** all its life, and the neck is covered in **pointed bumps**. Females grow to 28 cm of shell, males to about 18 cm. It is mainly a meat-eater, taking fish, tadpoles, frogs and crustaceans, and it will even tear up and eat cane toads. It can give off a strong smell and **bites hard** when handled [ref:wp-sawshell].

sections.heading: What it can be confused with
sections.body:
- **Northern yellow-faced turtle**: short neck, a yellow stripe from the eye back and another from the mouth along the neck, smooth shell edge [ref:wp-emydura].
- **Saw-shelled turtle**: the back edge of the shell stays saw-toothed for life and the neck carries pointed bumps; it bites hard [ref:wp-sawshell].
- **Northern snake-necked turtle**: a neck as long as the shell, folded sideways [ref:ala].
- **Snapping turtles** (*Elseya*): big and heavy-headed [ref:ala].

In the water, what you usually see is a head and nostrils at the surface, then nothing. The length of the neck and the shape of the head are the quickest tells.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Basking** on logs, rock bars and banks in the sun, and sliding off at the first movement on the bank. In the hot months they bask at night as well [ref:basking2023].
- **Heads at the surface** in the still water of the pool in the middle of the day.
- **Tracks**: paired flipper drags with a tail line between, running from the water to a nest hole dug in a sand bank from September to December [ref:wp-sawshell].
- **Dug-out nests**: a scatter of leathery shell fragments beside a hole is a nest found by a [goanna](entry:goanna) or a pig.
- **Empty freshwater mussel shells** on the bottom: the turtles are among the animals that open them [ref:turtle-competition].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: River turtles live in the permanent pools, slow reaches, billabongs and [paperbark](entry:paperbark) swamps of the rivers [ref:wp-emydura]. The saw-shelled turtle ranges through rivers, streams, swamps and lagoons from Cape York to northern New South Wales [ref:wp-sawshell].

sections.heading: Who eats whom, and when
sections.body:
The river turtles are the bottom workers of the [waterhole](entry:waterhole). Australia's short-necked turtles (*Emydura* and *Myuchelys*) are omnivores: in clear water much of their food comes from the invertebrates on the bottom, snails, [mussels](entry:mussels), insect larvae and small crustaceans; in muddy water they take more filamentous algae and more land insects that fall in [ref:turtle-competition]. A relative switches to a meat diet when plant food runs short [ref:turtle-competition]. The saw-shelled turtle is the hunter of the two: fish, tadpoles, [frogs](entry:frogs) and crustaceans, and it tears up and eats cane toads that kill most other animals [ref:wp-sawshell]. So the turtles share the catfish's food, the snails and insect larvae of the sand, and take the small [cherabin](entry:cherabin) and dead fish the pool offers.

**Who eats the turtle.** The [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile): turtles become a bigger part of its diet as it grows [ref:tucker1996]. Eggs and hatchlings go to [goannas](entry:goanna), kites, pigs and big fish; the adults' shell and bite are their defence [ref:wp-sawshell]. People took turtles in the dry season, by hand, by diving and on lines [ref:anderson1996].

**Hour and season.** Turtles work by day, feeding on the bottom and basking between feeds; the sources used here do not give a night-time account of the Mitchell species. Their year follows the pool: the dry season concentrates them in the permanent pools, where Bloomfield families went for them [ref:anderson1996]; nesting runs from September to December, with the eggs hatching in about 60 days, so the hatchlings arrive with the first floods [ref:wp-sawshell].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Saw-shelled turtles nest from **September to December**, laying several clutches of 9–20 eggs that hatch in about 60 days [ref:wp-sawshell]. Roth recorded that across North Queensland turtle eggs were eaten 'whenever found' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body: **Meat and eggs.** Ngujay was hunted for food. Its eggs (*[diburr](word:diburr)*, which also means 'seed') were eaten too [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]. The dictionary's word *[minya](word:minya)* covers 'meat, eggs (protein food)' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How it was caught and cooked
sections.body:
**By hand and with small [nets](entry:nets) (North Queensland generally).** Roth's summary is simple: 'Tortoises are caught in the hands or with small nets' [ref:roth1901]. His small folding hand-nets, described for fish, were worked by one person groping about the shallower waterholes with the net held in front or at the side [ref:roth1901].

**Feeling with the feet.** Roth recorded people groping carefully along the mud with their feet to catch catfish on the Georgina River [ref:roth1901]. None of the sources describes feeling for turtles the same way.

**Killing.** Two neighbouring methods are recorded [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Palmer River (Koko-minni):** pull the head well forwards, then **break the neck upwards and backwards**.
2. **Behind Princess Charlotte Bay:** push a stiff wooden bristle through the nostril into the brain and spinal cavity, and work it up and down.

**Cooking.** At Bloomfield, reptiles were cooked **straight on the fire** after the body had been bashed with an axe to break the bones [ref:anderson1996]. Roth describes the simplest cooking as laying the food 'on and in the hot ashes' [ref:roth1901], the dictionary's *[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals'; *[nulu](word:nulu)* is 'ashes' and *[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)* 'hot coals or hot ashes' [ref:hershberger1982]. Bigger animals went into the [stone oven](entry:earth-oven) (*[kurrma](word:kurrma)*). Hot stones were lifted with lawyer-cane tongs into a pit, and the meat, with eucalyptus, acacia or wild-ginger leaves, was set in a bark trough on the stones. More hot stones went around and on top, then [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark), and everything was covered with sand or earth for several hours [ref:anderson1996]. Food that is 'well cooked, done' is *[jani](word:jani)* [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Turtles bite.** The saw-shelled turtle bites hard when handled [ref:wp-sawshell]. Keep fingers away from the head.

**Crocodile water.** Diving and groping in waterholes is exactly what Crocwise warns against wherever [saltwater crocodiles](entry:saltwater-crocodile) could be: in croc country, keep out of the water and stay well back from the edge [ref:crocwise].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**The law.** Freshwater turtles are protected native animals under Queensland's *Nature Conservation Act 1992*, and anyone else needs a licence or permit to take them [ref:qld-nca]. If a turtle takes your bait, unhook it gently and let it go.

Native title holders' rights differ from place to place: see each place above, and ask the Traditional Owners before hunting, fishing or gathering.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[ngujay](word:ngujay)* 'freshwater turtle'; *[ngawiya](word:ngawiya)* '[sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle)'; *[kadan](word:kadan)* 'shell of turtle'; *[diburr](word:diburr)* 'egg'; *[jamal](word:jamal)* 'white of egg'; *[birukay](word:birukay)* 'yolk of the egg'; *[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)* 'good diver'; *[baral](word:baral)* 'to feel something', as in *nyulu nguwul-nguwulbu torch baran-baral* 'He was feeling for his torch in the dark' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Turtles are food on the Hann. A Thaypan man told the Federal Court: 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan]. Four kinds are on record around the middle Hann, two short-necked and two long-necked [ref:ala-hann-turtle], and Kuku Thaypan Elders read the fat long-neck turtle as a sign of the season [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Which turtles live here
sections.body: The Atlas of Living Australia holds 57 freshwater turtle records (1968–2025) in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru. The commonest is **Krefft's river turtle** (*Emydura macquarii*, 27 records), then the **saw-shelled turtle** (10), the **northern snake-necked turtle** (*Chelodina rugosa*, 8) and **Cann's snake-necked turtle** (*Chelodina canni*, 6) [ref:ala-hann-turtle]. The northern yellow-faced turtle described above is not among them. Look for them in the deep permanent holes of the river and in the lagoons.

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: In the dry, the deep permanent waterholes of Rinyirru hold 'waterbirds, turtles and crocodiles'. There 'long-necked turtles are also ambush hunters. They sometimes conceal themselves in sediment at the bottom of the waterhole and, using their long neck, strike with speed and accuracy, engulfing small fish and shrimps' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The crocodiles of those holes take turtles too [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Hann never stops running, so its holes hold water through the late dry [ref:bom-105001b]. Feral pigs are a threat: around swamps they 'dig up large areas of soil, eat the bulbs of water lilies and turtle eggs' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body: Kuku Thaypan Elders read the country's signs to time their burning. In the lead-up to the burning season, when the wetlands begin drying out (about January to April), their indicators include **Nye Koil**, the 'Longneck Freshwater Turtle', being fat, alongside 'Fat Goanna' and 'Healthy Possums' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: How people used it here
sections.body:
**Thaypan and Possum.** 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan]. A man who identifies as Thaypan and Possum said: 'I have rights to take resources without permission in my traditional areas. Like fishing, and turtle, camping, cutting trees, take animals etc.' He added: 'There are strict rules that you don't take too much' [ref:fca-thaypan] [ref:fca-possum].

**Kuku Warra (Laura).** A Kuku Warra man gave the Court his knowledge of 'hunting, cooking and eating different types of turtle' [ref:fca-kukuwarra].

**Roth, about 1900.** The two killing methods described above come from this side of the range: behind Princess Charlotte Bay a stiff wooden bristle was pushed through the nostril, and on the Palmer the neck was broken [ref:roth1901].

**Story.** The long-necked turtle has a place in the stories of Rinyirru, told by its Traditional Owners [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Those stories belong to their custodians.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, both recognised in November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Turtles are protected, but native title holders taking them for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs do not need the licences others need [ref:nta1993]. Rinyirru's Traditional Owners are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

locations.summary: The upper Mitchell around [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is turtle country, with northern yellow-faced and saw-shelled turtles the commonest kinds on record [ref:ala].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: The Atlas of Living Australia has northern yellow-faced turtle records within 30 km of the [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) homestead, one of them about 11 km to the west, and a snapping turtle (*Elseya*) recorded about 25 km to the south-east. About 30 km east, on the Mitchell, a 1973 museum survey collected large series of both northern yellow-faced and saw-shelled turtles. A northern snake-necked turtle and a few Krefft's turtles have also been recorded in the upper Mitchell country [ref:ala]. Look for them in the long, permanent pools of the river.

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: The crocodile recorded around Karma Waters is the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile), *[ngawurr-ngawun](word:ngawurr-ngawun)* [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:ala]. It is usually shy, but a big one can give a serious bite [ref:am-johnstoni].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
**Native title.** The 2013 Western Yalanji determinations recognise rights to **hunt, fish and gather on the land and waters for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes** [ref:brady2013]. A further Western Yalanji determination followed in August 2026 [ref:nit2026wy]. Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* means native title holders hunting for those needs do not need the licences and permits other people need [ref:alrc].

**At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters).** The station's agreement with the Western Yalanji Traditional Owners was the first on pastoral land in Australia [ref:karma]. Ask the Traditional Owners before taking anything from their country, and follow the station's rules: no weapons or hunting dogs, and no recreation access from 1 December to 1 April [ref:karma-camping].

**At Karma Waters.** Karma Waters Station falls under the earlier 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. See the [Karma Waters guide](/dictionaries/kuku_yalanji/country/places/karma-waters) for what it covers, and ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting, fishing or gathering.

locations.summary: Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji went to the freshwater streams for '[eelfish](entry:eels) and freshwater tortoise', especially in the [dry season](entry:seasons) [ref:anderson1996]. They caught turtles on bark [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) with [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn hooks, and by the 1970s by diving with goggles and a steel rod [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body: At Bloomfield, freshwater tortoise was a **dry-season** food. Inland groups, which camped on sandy creek beds in the dry, split into small family groups and set up temporary 'branch' camps to go after [eelfish](entry:eels), tortoises, [wallabies](entry:wallaby) and [goannas](entry:goanna). Coastal people made seasonal trips inland to the freshwater streams 'for eelfish and freshwater tortoise' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Uses here
sections.body: At Bloomfield ngujay was one of the foods small family groups went after from their temporary dry-season camps [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: How it was caught here
sections.body:
**[Hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines) (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji)** [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Make a line from the bark of *Sterculia quadrifolia*.
2. Make a hook from a **[lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn**.
3. Bait it with [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub), [small freshwater prawns](entry:cherabin) or small [frogs](entry:frogs).
4. Fish the freshwater creeks and waterholes. Lines were used here for turtle, [eelfish](entry:eels), [catfish](entry:catfish) and perch, and this was mostly women's work.

**Diving (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji, late 1970s).** In the inland creeks people dived for freshwater eelfish and turtles, using **diving goggles and a flexible steel rod** [ref:anderson1996]. *[Mala-kural](word:mala-kural)* is 'a good diver' [ref:hershberger1982].
